questions.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3}+{y}^{2},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & ∗ \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}y+{y}^{3} & {x}^{3}+3x{y}^{2}+2y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}6xy & 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & 6xy+2\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+3+(x-1)=2x+1.
$$

questions.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-y},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & ∗ \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2x+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y} \\ -{e}^{x-y} & {e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+(-1)+(x-1)=2x-3.
$$

questions.problem:
For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{e}^{y}),$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=ax+by-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+cxy.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{y}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{{e}^{y}}{x+{e}^{y}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{x{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈0+1\cdot x+1\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-1)\cdot xy+0\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1x+1y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(-1)xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+(-1)=1.
$$

questions.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1,1) & =1, & \,{f}^{′}(0,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(0,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(1,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,2,1) & ≈1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2-1 \\ 1-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2-1 \\ 1-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2-1 \\ 1-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =1+1+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =2+\frac{1}{2}(2) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\pi ,1,0) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(\pi ,1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(\pi ,1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}\pi  \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(\pi ,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}\pi  \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\pi  \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-\pi  \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\pi  \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}\pi  \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\pi ,0,1) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\pi -\pi  \\ 0-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}\pi -\pi  \\ 0-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\pi -\pi  \\ 0-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+1+\pi +\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\pi +\frac{1}{2}(3) \\  & =\pi +\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
